name: Dinka, Northern/Padang variety within a pan-Dinka analysis
confidence_why: Malou 1988, Tucker & Bryan 1966 and Blum 2023 all describe Dinka, including the Padang and Ngok varieties, as a tone language with three or four contrastive tones, and the only disagreement concerns Malou's side remark that each word also carries one non-contrastive stress of unstudied placement, which acoustic work on other dialects reported by Remijsen & Manyang 2009 and by van Urk & Chong 2025…

It is clear, however, that stress is neither contrastive nor used at all in connection w…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dinka (all four major varieties, explicitly including Northern/Padang) has exactly one culminative stress per phonological word; the source does not say which syllable carries it ('the factors that condition stress have not been studied'), only that stress is non-contrastive and not used for emphasis. Lexical and morphological prosody is carried by tone, vowel length and voice quality (for the Ngok-Sobat variety of nort2815 see Blum 2023 ch.5: four tones L/H/HL/LH, three vowel lengths, two voice qualities). Later work on other Dinka varieties doubts a stress system altogether (Remijsen & Manyang 2009 fn.5: no acoustic support in Luanyjang; van Urk & Chong 2025: 'Dinka lacks an obvious stress system'); a 2025 instrumental investigation of Dinka stress (Blum et al. dataset) has no published result yet.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the author states that the conditioning factors have not been studied and that stress, juncture and intonation are outside the scope of the book.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (bounded by potential pause); the examples in (5), pp. 9-10, are two-word citation phrases each carrying a single stress mark (e.g. 'mony dit 'old man', ' yok lac 'pregnant cows'), so the statement concerns word-level prominence in citation forms, not phrase-level or sentence intonation (treated separately under 2.1 with downdrift).
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is pan-Dinka, not specific to Northeastern Dinka: Malou (1988: 1) says his analysis covers the four major varieties 'Eastern, which is Bor based; Northern, known as Padan, which is Donjol based; Southern which is Agar based; and Western which is Rek based', so the Northern/Padang variety (Dongjol, dong1295, a dialect of nort2815) is explicitly within scope, but the author's own variety is not stated (the reader for Southwestern Dinka's internal-evidence check suggests it is neither Rek nor Agar). The same Malou passage has been recorded for sout2832 (Southwestern) and sout2834 (Southeastern); the catalog should treat it as one source claim covering all Dinka lects rather than four independent descriptions. The only first-hand descriptions of nort2815 dialects proper are tone/length studies that do not mention stress: Blum 2023 ch.5 (Ngok of the Padang cluster, speakers from the Malakal area = Ngok-Sobat ngok1245; held by the project) and Remijsen 2014 (Ageer agee1238; abstract only).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's Malou 1988 statement (one stress per phonological word, conditioning factors unstudied, non-contrastive): Tucker & Bryan add a placement generalization (stem, never affixes), which Malou does not give. Scope caveat: the sentence is made for the four Nilotic heads together, not for Dinka alone; the chapter's Dinka examples are 'unless otherwise stated, from the BOR dialect' (Southeastern Dinka), with Padang entering only through 'R. Trudinger, Dinka Grammar, MS. (PADANG)' and scattered comparative forms (e.g. REK/PADANG/AGAR/BOR negative-verb forms); 'Ngok' has 0 hits in the volume. Probes pairing 'stress' with DINKA, NUER, SHILLUK, LWO, LANGO, ACOLI, REK, AGAR,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Nilotic languages treated jointly in the chapter (DINKA, NUER, N. LWO = Shilluk, S. LWO), stress falls on the word stem and never on a prefix or suffix; tone is separately lexical and grammatical (sec. 2a: three tone levels High, Mid, Low; 'In DINKA-NUER and SHILLUK at least there are three specific tonemes'). No Dinka-specific or Padang-specific stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Dinka; a possible relationship between stress and vowel length is noted for Southern Lwo only (cross-reference § 14 (i)).
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan 1966 treat DINKA, NUER, Northern Lwo (Shilluk) and Southern Lwo jointly; Dinka examples are from the Bor dialect (Southeastern Dinka) unless otherwise stated, and Padang (the nort2815 cluster) appears only as a manuscript source (Trudinger) and in a few comparative forms; Ngok is not named. Malou 1988 (catalog source) is pan-Dinka and explicitly includes 'Northern, known as Padan[g], which is Donjol based' (= Dongjol, under nort2815). Blum 2023 ch. 5 describes Ngok (Padang cluster) tone only, with no stress statement.

readall_conflicts: No two opened sources give different placements: Malou 1988 (catalog) gives no placement and says stress is non-contrastive with unstudied conditioning; Tucker & Bryan 1966 (snippets, group-level for Nilotic) put stress on the stem and never on affixes, which is compatible and, for a 'largely monosyllabic' language (Blum 2023, sec. 2.2.1), nearly vacuous. Gilley 2004 was not opened. A tension exists with later instrumental work already held by the project in the sibling Dinka directories but not among this item's listed works: Remijsen & Manyang 2009 (fn. 5: Gilley's 2003 'stress' is the morphological short grade, and Remijsen & Gilley 2008 found no acoustic support in Luanyjang) and van Urk & Chong 2025 ('Dinka lacks an obvious stress system'), which cast doubt on whether Dinka has word stress at all; Blum et al. 2025 announce a stress dataset with no stated result. None of these concerns the Padang cluster specifically.
